title: Bifidobacterium Longum Probiotic: How to Read the Label
summary: A Bifidobacterium longum probiotic label names a species, not a strain. Learn what parents can and cannot tell from that name.
body_markdown:
A Bifidobacterium longum probiotic label answers one narrow question: which species of bacteria the maker is naming. It does not tell you the subspecies, the strain, the age group studied, or whether that organism is the one in a paper you just read. Parents run into the name on infant and toddler supplements because Bifidobacterium is common in early-life gut research. The useful next step is to read the rest of the label before treating two products as the same.


[See how Persephone describes its strains](https://persephone.bio/pages/our-science)


## What a Bifidobacterium longum probiotic name actually says


Bifidobacterium longum is one species in the genus Bifidobacterium. The genus is the wider group. The species is a single member of that group. Researchers describe B. longum as a rod-shaped bacterium that lives in the human gut, next to many other Bifidobacterium species. A species on a supplement label points to that member. It does not point to the whole genus.


Three levels show up on careful labels. They are easy to collapse into one.


- **Genus:** Bifidobacterium, the wider family name parents also see on B. breve and B. bifidum products.
- **Species:** longum, the specific species in the name Bifidobacterium longum.
- **Strain:** an extra code after the species, such as a number or letter string, that points to one member of that species.


A Bifidobacterium longum probiotic listing that stops at the species has completed only the middle step. Two products can both say B. longum and still name different strains, different amounts, and different companion ingredients. Species-level similarity is not evidence that the products were studied in the same way.


For a plain introduction to the organisms behind these names, start with[meet the beneficial microbes](https://persephone.bio/blogs/news/meet-the-microbes) . If you want the broader infant context rather than this species, the[guide to probiotics for babies](https://persephone.bio/blogs/news/probiotics-for-babies) is the better next read.


## Why subspecies sit between the species and the strain


The species name has a history that still confuses labels. In 2002, microbiologists grouped three organisms that had been separate species into one species called Bifidobacterium longum. Those three were B. longum, B. infantis, and B. suis. They kept the older names as biotypes. In 2008, Mattarelli and colleagues proposed three subspecies instead: B. longum subsp. longum, B. longum subsp. infantis, and B. longum subsp. suis. The taxonomy subcommittee favored that proposal. The paper is indexed on[PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18398167/) .


That history matters on a shopping label for a simple reason. A line that says only "Bifidobacterium longum" does not tell you which subspecies is meant. Do not assume the product is B. infantis just because infantis was folded into the species. Do not assume it is subsp. longum just because that name looks like the default. The label has to say so.


Subspecies are not a trivia detail. A 2008 genome paper looked at one infantis strain, ATCC 15697. It described a large set of genes for using milk oligosaccharides, the complex sugars in human milk. That finding belongs to the strain that was sequenced. You cannot assign it to every organism filed under Bifidobacterium longum. The paper is indexed on[PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19033196/) .


Parents comparing B. longum with B. breve, rather than reading one species, already have a separate article:[B. breve and B. longum compared](https://persephone.bio/blogs/news/bifidobacterium-breve-vs-bifidobacterium-longum-for-babies) . This page stays with the longum name itself.


## How commercial labels use the same species name differently


The National Institutes of Health keeps a Dietary Supplement Label Database. It files Bifidobacterium longum as a bacteria ingredient. Under that one record, labels use the bare species name and the species name plus an extra code. Public examples include BB536, 1714, and ATCC culture numbers. The record is here:[Bifidobacterium longum in the DSLD](https://dsld.od.nih.gov/ingredient/Bifidobacterium%20longum) .


Those extra codes are the point. They show that "Bifidobacterium longum" is a shared species name, and the characters after it are what separate one labeled organism from another. A code is still only an identity tag. It does not tell you the study population, the dose, or the rest of the formula.


If a label names the strain 1714 and you want to know what that particular identifier does and does not prove, use the[Bifidobacterium Longum guide](https://persephone.bio/blogs/news/bifidobacterium-longum-1714) . This article does not walk through that strain. It stops at the species, so the strain page can do the narrower job.


What the label shows What you can say What you still need


Bifidobacterium only. The genus, not a species. The species name, and a strain if the maker has one.


Bifidobacterium longum. The species, shared by many strains. Subspecies and strain, if either is specified.


B. longum subsp. infantis or subsp. longum. Which subspecies the maker claims. The strain code and the evidence for that strain.


B. longum plus a strain code. A specific named member of the species. Whether research used that strain, that amount, and a comparable age group.


## Why the species on a label is not the same as the organism in a study


A practical check comes from outside any one brand. In Pediatric Research, Lewis and colleagues evaluated 16 probiotic products to see whether the bifidobacteria detected in the product matched the species on the label. Only one of the 16 matched its bifidobacterial label claims in every sample tested, and the products varied from pill to pill and from lot to lot. The paper is[Validating bifidobacterial species and subspecies identity in commercial probiotic products](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26571226/) .


Read that result narrowly. It does not mean most products on the shelf today are mislabeled. It does not score any current infant formula. It does show why copying a species name from a study onto a product panel is not enough. The authors also make a distinction parents can use. B. longum subsp. longum and B. longum subsp. infantis are not interchangeable just because both carry the species name.


Hold a study next to a label. Line up four facts before you decide the paper is about that product:


- The full name in the methods. That includes subspecies and strain, not the short name in the headline.
- Who was studied, including age. Adult or animal findings do not automatically describe healthy full-term infants or toddlers.
- The preparation researchers used: the strain, the amount, and any prebiotic or other ingredient given with it.
- The question the study actually measured. A paper about identity, survival, or microbial change is not a promise about how an individual child will feel.


Persephone's own writing on[proprietary probiotic strains](https://persephone.bio/blogs/news/bifidobacterium-products-proprietary-strain) goes further into why a strain designation is the level that makes a comparison fair.


## Where B. longum fits in an infant or toddler synbiotic


A probiotic is the live microorganism. A prebiotic is food for that microorganism. A synbiotic is the combination. Persephone uses "synergistic synbiotic" in the scientific sense. The strains and the prebiotic sugars were chosen to work as a pair, not as a slogan. Both formulas use human milk oligosaccharides, HMOs, from all three structural classes found in breast milk. The[guide to how HMOs pair with probiotics](https://persephone.bio/blogs/news/what-are-hmos-and-why-they-matter-in-our-synbiotic) explains that half of the formula.


On the[Our Science](https://persephone.bio/pages/our-science) page, Persephone identifies four proprietary Bifidobacterium strains in its infant and toddler powders:


- PB-01 and PB-02, both B. infantis, described as strong users of HMOs.
- PB-03, B. longum. Persephone describes this strain as able to use HMOs and other carbohydrates, and ties it to the move toward solid foods and to gut barrier function.
- PB-04, B. breve, described as helping break down complex carbohydrates.


PB-03 is one named B. longum strain inside a four-strain blend. It is not a stand-in for every Bifidobacterium longum probiotic on the market. It is not the same organism as 1714 or any other public strain code. If a label does not list PB-03, research or copy about PB-03 does not transfer to it.


The infant powder is for healthy full-term babies from birth through 12 months. It is flavorless. It pairs the four strains with four HMOs and 400 IU of vitamin D3. The listed probiotic amount is 1 billion AFU.


The toddler powder is for ages 12 to 36 months. It uses the same four strains at 5 billion AFU, with 1 gram of the HMO blend and the same 400 IU of vitamin D3. The first direct order carries a 60-day Peace of Mind Promise.


Those statements have not been evaluated by the FDA. This product is not intended to diagnose, treat, cure, or prevent any disease.


Persephone's starting evidence is the My Baby Biome Study. Researchers analyzed more than 400 diapers. They reported that 9 in 10 U.S. infants were missing one or more keystone Bifidobacterium strains. Jarman and colleagues published that result in Communications Biology in 2025. The paper describes what the study measured. It is not a claim that a product prevents illness, and it is not a judgment about how any parent feeds their baby. Details sit on[the My Baby Biome study explained](https://persephone.bio/blogs/news/our-my-baby-biome-study-explained) .


## How to read a Bifidobacterium longum probiotic label


Use the same pass every time the species name shows up. That includes a box, a product page, or a social post.


1. Find the full microbial name. If you only see the genus, or only the species, you do not yet know the strain.
2. Look for a subspecies. If infantis or longum appears after "subsp.", write that down. If it does not appear, do not fill it in yourself.
3. Copy the strain code exactly, including letters and numbers. Then check whether any cited paper uses that same code.
4. Check the age on the evidence and the age on the product. Healthy full-term infants and toddlers are not the same group as adults.
5. Read the other ingredients. A strain studied alone is not the same mix as a strain paired with HMOs or other species.
6. Note the amount and the unit. AFU and CFU are different counting methods. Match the number to the serving the label tells you to use.


For the infant powder, mix the packet into the bottle while you prepare it, as long as the milk is not too hot. Do not add the powder partway through a feeding. Storage, testing, and pediatrician questions are on the[Persephone FAQ](https://persephone.bio/pages/faq) and the[safety page](https://persephone.bio/pages/safety) . A supplement label is not personal medical advice.


[Read the Bifidobacterium Longum guide](https://persephone.bio/blogs/news/bifidobacterium-longum-1714)


That guide covers one strain identifier. It is not a product page. When you are ready to see how Persephone uses its own B. longum strain, PB-03, inside a four-strain synbiotic, start with the age on the label. The[infant synbiotic for healthy full-term babies](https://persephone.bio/products/bloom) is for birth through 12 months. The[toddler synbiotic](https://persephone.bio/products/thrive) is for 12 to 36 months. Both are flavorless powders with the same four Bifidobacterium strains, four HMOs, and 400 IU of vitamin D3. Questions about fit for your child belong with your pediatrician, or with the[Persephone team](https://persephone.bio/pages/contact) .


## Frequently asked questions


### Is every Bifidobacterium longum probiotic the same strain?


No. Bifidobacterium longum is the species. A strain is a more specific member, usually shown as an extra code. Two products can list the species and still contain different strains. Match the full name before you treat a paper about one strain as a paper about the other.


### Does B. longum on a label mean B. infantis?


Not by itself. B. infantis is a subspecies, written B. longum subsp. infantis. A 2008 proposal split the species that way. A label that stops at Bifidobacterium longum has not named a subspecies. Look for "subsp. infantis," or for a strain the company identifies as infantis.


### What is the difference between a probiotic and a synbiotic?


A probiotic is the beneficial microorganism. A prebiotic is food for it, such as the HMOs in these formulas. A synbiotic contains both. The infant and toddler powders pair four Bifidobacterium strains with four HMOs chosen for those strains, plus 400 IU of vitamin D3.


### Is B. longum PB-03 the same as Bifidobacterium longum 1714?


No. PB-03 is Persephone's proprietary B. longum strain in the infant and toddler formulations. 1714 is a different strain identifier. Sharing the species name does not make them the same organism or give them the same evidence. The strain guide linked above is the place to read about 1714.


### Can this species name tell me if a product is right for my baby?


It cannot. The species only names a group of bacteria. Fit also depends on the strain, the full formula, the age range, and your pediatrician. The infant powder is for healthy full-term babies from 0 to 12 months. The toddler powder is for 12 to 36 months. These statements have not been evaluated by the FDA. This product is not intended to diagnose, treat, cure, or prevent any disease.
